# SDMs with tidymodels for time-scattered and palaeo data

In this article, we show how a Species Distribution Model can be fitted
with `tidysdm` on time-scattered (i.e.palaeontological,
archaeozoological, archaeological, but also focusing on recent climate
changes, e.g. historical specimens) data, with samples covering
different time periods. 
Here we show the full workflow, from preparing the data to performing ensemble modelling and projections for time-scattered occurrences. The first stages are also
fully described in the ["tidysdm overview"
article](https://evolecolgroup.github.io/tidysdm/dev/articles/tidysdm.html),
which focuses on present data. @TODO update link according to dev/main

We first load `tidysdm`:

```{r}
library(tidysdm)
```

# Preparing your data

We start by loading a set of georeferenced radiocarbon dates (calibrated) for horses,
spanning from 22k years ago until 8k years ago.

```{r load_presences}
data(horses)
horses
```

`tidysdm` works with `sf` objects to represent locations, so we will cast our
coordinates into an `sf` object, and set its projections to standard
'lonlat' using the proj4 string "+proj=longlat".
We convert our dataset into an `sf` data.frame so that we can easily
plot it (here `tidyterra` shines):

```{r}
library(sf)
horses <- st_as_sf(horses, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"))
st_crs(horses) <- 4326
```

It is usually advisable to plot the locations directly on the raster
that will be used to extract climatic variables, to see how the
locations fall within the discrete space of the raster. 
We can access palaeoclimatic reconstructions through the package [`pastclim`](https://evolecolgroup.github.io/pastclim/).
In this case, we will use its Example dataset which only includes a small number of variables and time steps (more information on datasets can be found [here](https://evolecolgroup.github.io/pastclim/articles/a1_available_datasets.html)).

As a first step, we will plot our presences against the land mask for the
present, taken from `pastclim`. We will use a polygon already included in `pastclim` to cut the map and cover only Europe:

```{r echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
library(pastclim)
set_data_path(on_CRAN = TRUE)
```

```{r}
library(pastclim)
land_mask <- pastclim::get_land_mask(time_bp = 0, dataset = "Example")
# extension for Europe from pastclim
europe_poly <- vect(region_outline$Europe)
crs(europe_poly) <- "lonlat"
# crop the extent
land_mask <- crop(land_mask, europe_poly)
# and mask to the polygon
land_mask <- mask(land_mask, europe_poly)
```

For plotting, we can use `tidyterra`, which easily handles `terra` rasters with `ggplot`:

```{r cast_to_sf, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
library(tidyterra)
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = land_mask, aes(fill = land_mask_0),
                  use_coltab = FALSE) +
  geom_sf(data = horses, aes(col = time_bp)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = "cornsilk3", na.value = "transparent")
```

# Map projection
We need to make sure that all our data (points and rasters) have the same geographic coordinate reference system (CRS) by projecting them. In some of the pipeline steps (e.g. thinning data, measuring areas) using an equal area projection may make a significant difference, especially for large-scale projects.

You can use the R package `crstools` (https://evolecolgroup.github.io/crstools/index.html, also available on [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/crstools/index.html))
to find an appropriate equal area [projection](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-51835-0_9) for any region. 

The CRS for this object in Proj4 code is:
```{r check_crs_proj4}
sf::st_crs(land_mask)$proj4string
```

use `suggest_crs()` to get a suggestion for an equal-area CRS for this map:
```{r find_crs}
library(crstools)
land_mask_equal_area <- suggest_crs(land_mask, distortion = "equal_area")
# keep Proj4
europe_proj4 <- land_mask_equal_area$proj4
```

For rasters (maps), we use the `terra` function `project` to change the CRS. We pass the raster object and the proj4 string as arguments:

```{r}
land_mask_proj <- terra::project(land_mask, y = europe_proj4)
```

Now we need to project the data points to the same CRS as the raster. We will do so using the appropriate `sf` function:

```{r}
horses_proj <- st_transform(horses, europe_proj4)
```

Plotting the data, we will see that the shape of the land mask has changed following the new projection.

```{r project_iberia, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = land_mask_proj, aes(fill = land_mask_0),
                  use_coltab = FALSE) +
  geom_sf(data = horses_proj, aes(col = time_bp)) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = "cornsilk3", na.value = "transparent")
```

# Getting the climate data

We now need a time series of palaeoclimate reconstructions, not just a land mask. We will use the Example dataset from `pastclim`, as mentioned before. 
This dataset only has reconstructions every 5k years for the past 20k years at 1
degree resolution, with 3 bioclimatic variables. It will suffice for
illustrative purposes, but we recommend that you download higher quality
datasets with `pastclim` for real analysis. As for the land mask, we
will cut the reconstructions to cover Europe only:

```{r load_climate}
library(pastclim)
climate_vars <- c("bio01", "bio10", "bio12")
climate_full <- pastclim::region_series(
  bio_variables = climate_vars,
  data = "Example",
  crop = region_outline$Europe
)
```

and then project:
```{r}
# climate_full is SpatRasterDataset, so we need to update every layer
climate_full_proj_bio01 <- terra::project(climate_full[["bio01"]], europe_proj4)
terra::plot(climate_full_proj_bio01)

# you can do this in a loop for all the layers
climate_full_proj <- lapply(climate_vars, function(var) {
  terra::project(climate_full[[var]], europe_proj4)
})

climate_full_proj <- terra::sds(climate_full_proj)
names(climate_full_proj) <- climate_vars
```



# Thinning step

Often data tend to be spatially or chronologically structured, i.e. we have way more samples from specific regions and/or time periods. This could result in an imbalance that may bias our results. This can be dealt with by thinning the data. Thinning means removing points that are too close to others (either spatially or chronologically), thus avoiding oversampling (and sampling biases).

There are different options for thinning your data: a) considering the resolution of the climate data (i.e. keeping one point in each cell), b) considering the distance between points (spatial and chronological). 

We thin the observations to only keep one per cell in the raster, and remove
locations outside the desired area (if there was any):

```{r thin_by_cell}
set.seed(123)
horses_thin <- thin_by_cell_time(horses_proj,
  raster = climate_full_proj,
  time_col = "time_bp",
  lubridate_fun = pastclim::ybp2date
)
nrow(horses)
```

Let's see what we have left of our points:

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = land_mask_proj, aes(fill = land_mask_0),
                  use_coltab = FALSE) +
  geom_sf(data = horses_thin, aes(col = time_bp)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = "cornsilk3", na.value = "transparent")
```


There are still geographic clusters of points of similar age, so we could also consider further thinning the data based on minimum distance. The following block shows how we thin our data to remove presences that are closer than 200km and less than 2000 years apart. As the units
of our projection are m (the default for most projections), we use
a convenient conversion function, `km2m()` to input kilometers, and a conversion for years to days (`y2d()`) to
avoid having to write lots of zeroes:
```{r thin_by_dist}
set.seed(123)
horses_dist <- thin_by_dist_time(horses_thin,
  dist_min = km2m(200),
  interval_min = y2d(2000),
  time_col = "time_bp",
  # convert time column into a lubridate object (format for date-time data)
  lubridate_fun = pastclim::ybp2date
)
nrow(horses_dist)
```

And see what we have left:

```{r plot_thinned, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = land_mask_proj, aes(fill = land_mask_0),
                  use_coltab = FALSE) +
  geom_sf(data = horses_dist, aes(col = time_bp)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = "cornsilk3", na.value = "transparent")
```


# Sample pseudo-absences

We now need to select points that represent the potential available area for the species. There are two approaches, we can either sample the background (i.e. points sampled from the whole area considered potentially including presences) with `sample_background()`, or we can generate pseudo-absences (i.e. points where the species has not been observed) with `sample_pseudoabs()`. 

In this vignette, we sample pseudo-absences (we will constraint them to be at least
70km away from any presences), selecting three times the number of
presences.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
horses_pa <- sample_pseudoabs_time(horses_dist,
  n_per_presence = 3,
  raster = climate_full_proj,
  time_col = "time_bp",
  lubridate_fun = pastclim::ybp2date,
  method = c("dist_min", km2m(70))
)
```

Let's see our presences and pseudo-absences:

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = land_mask_proj, aes(fill = land_mask_0),
                  use_coltab = FALSE) +
  geom_sf(data = horses_pa, aes(col = class)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = "cornsilk3", na.value = "transparent")
```

Now let's get the climate for these location. `pastclim` requires a data
frame with two columns with coordinates and a column of time in years
before present (where negative values represent time in the past). We
manipulate the `sf` object accordingly:

```{r climate_for_locations}
# reformatting the object (excluding geometry column)
horses_df <- horses_pa %>%
  dplyr::bind_cols(sf::st_coordinates(horses_pa)) %>%
  mutate(time_bp = date2ybp(time_step)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  select(-geometry)
# get climate
horses_df <- location_slice_from_region_series(horses_df,
  region_series = climate_full_proj
)

# add the climate reconstructions to the sf object, and remove the time_step
# as we don't need it for modelling
horses_climate <- horses_pa %>%
  bind_cols(horses_df[, climate_vars]) %>%
  select(-time_step)
```

# Fit the model by crossvalidation

Next, we need to set up a `recipe` to define how to handle our dataset.
We don't want to transform our data, so we just need to define the
formula (*class* is the outcome, all other variables are predictors;
note that, for `sf` objects, `geometry` is automatically ignored as a
predictor):

```{r recipe}
horses_rec <- recipe(horses_climate, formula = class ~ .)
horses_rec
```

We can quickly check that we have the variables that we want with:

```{r}
horses_rec$var_info
```

We now build a `workflow_set` of different models, defining which
hyperparameters we want to tune. We will use *glm*, *gam*, *random
forest* and *boosted trees* as our models, so only *random forest* and
*boosted trees* have tunable hyperparameters. For the most commonly used
models, `tidysdm` automatically chooses the most important parameters,
but it is possible to fully customise model specifications.

```{r workflow_set}
horses_models <-
  # create the workflow_set
  workflow_set(
    preproc = list(default = horses_rec),
    models = list(
      # the standard glm specs  (no params to tune)
      glm = sdm_spec_glm(),
      # the standard sdm specs (no params to tune)
      gam = sdm_spec_gam(),
      # rf specs with tuning
      rf = sdm_spec_rf(),
      # boosted tree model (gbm) specs with tuning
      gbm = sdm_spec_boost_tree()
    ),
    # make all combinations of preproc and models,
    cross = TRUE
  ) %>%
  # set formula for gams
  update_workflow_model("default_gam",
    spec = sdm_spec_gam(),
    formula = gam_formula(horses_rec)
  ) %>%
  # tweak controls to store information needed later to create the ensemble
  option_add(control = control_ensemble_grid())
```

Note that *gams* are unusual, as we need to specify a formula to define
to which variables we will fit smooths. By default, `gam_formula()` fits
a smooth to every continuous predictor, but a custom formula can be
provided instead.

We now want to set up a spatial block cross-validation scheme to tune
and assess our models:

```{r training_cv, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
library(tidysdm)
set.seed(1005)
horses_cv <- spatial_block_cv(horses_climate, v = 5)
autoplot(horses_cv)
```

We can now use the block CV folds to tune and assess the models:

```{r tune_grid}
set.seed(123)
horses_models <-
  horses_models %>%
  workflow_map("tune_grid",
    resamples = horses_cv, grid = 5,
    metrics = sdm_metric_set(), verbose = TRUE
  )
```

Note that `workflow_set` correctly detects that we have no tuning
parameters for *glm* and *gam*. We can have a look at the performance of
our models with:

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
autoplot(horses_models)
```

Now let's create an ensemble, selecting the best set of parameters for
each model (this is really only relevant for the random forest, as there
were not hype-parameters to tune for the glm and gam). We will use the
Boyce continuous index as our metric to choose the best random forest
and boosted tree. When adding members to an ensemble, they are
automatically fitted to the full training dataset, and so ready to make
predictions.

```{r}
horses_ensemble <- simple_ensemble() %>%
  add_member(horses_models, metric = "boyce_cont")
```

And visualise it

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
autoplot(horses_ensemble)
```

# Projecting to other times

We can now make predictions with this ensemble (using the default option
of taking the mean of the predictions from each model) for the Last
Glacial Maximum (LGM, 21,000 years ago).

```{r get_lgm}
climate_lgm <- pastclim::region_slice(
  time_bp = -20000,
  bio_variables = climate_vars,
  data = "Example",
  crop = region_outline$Europe
)
```

And predict using the ensemble:

```{r plot_lgm, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
prediction_lgm <- predict_raster(horses_ensemble, climate_lgm)
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = prediction_lgm, aes(fill = mean)) +
  scale_fill_terrain_c()
```
